summary: Describes the functional requirements for a routing protocol to run between autonomous systems. It is meant as a precursor to design of a new protocol, covering the DoD IP, ISO IP, and future Internet needs.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building a new road map system between big networks, this writes down what the system must be able to do.

subtitle: The wish list for a routing protocol between autonomous systems, written before the protocol itself was designed.

tldr.problem: The Internet was growing and its operators wanted independent control, so a new protocol for routing between autonomous systems was needed, but nobody had agreed what it should achieve.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists overall goals, grouped functional requirements, general objectives and explicit non-goals for inter-autonomous system routing, with an appendix that explains the issues behind them.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol. It does not specify a standard and was circulated for comment as the basis for a future routing architecture.

today: RFC 1126 is a requirements memo that says it does not specify a standard, and its status is recorded as Unknown with no obsoleting or updating RFCs in the unit metadata. It states that it is a precursor to design work, not a protocol.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1126 describes the goals and functional requirements for a routing protocol used between autonomous systems. It is meant as a necessary precursor to designing a new inter-autonomous system routing protocol, applicable to the current DoD IP, the ISO IP and future Internet protocols. It does not specify a standard.

The goals say what the architecture should accomplish as a whole. The functional requirements are more detailed and grouped by area. General objectives such as robustness follow, and things that are not reasonably attainable are named as non-requirements. The text is concise on purpose, with supporting arguments in an appendix. The work comes from the Open Routing Working Group, and the authors expect it to resemble needs seen in ANSI, ECMA and ISO environments.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a wish list for a way to send messages between very large networks, written before anyone builds it.

sections.title: The Eight Overall Goals
sections.content:
The memo sets eight high-level goals. Routing should deliver datagrams from one source to one or more destinations, including multi-homed hosts and multicast. It should be assured: when service cannot be provided, the requester is told on a best-effort basis, although this is not guaranteed delivery. The design should handle a large number of routing entities, growth for the next 10 years, and autonomous operation, so each administration can set its own policy for its own resources.

It should be a distributed system with no centralized or ubiquitous data repository, offer a credible and reasonably secure environment, be a managed entity that gives operators insight and control, and minimize the memory, transmission and processing it needs without assuming major technology upgrades.
sections.plainLanguage: The new system should get messages where they are going, say so when it cannot, work for a huge number of networks, let each owner make their own rules, and not need fancy new equipment.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
sections.content:
Requirements are grouped by area. Route synthesis (choosing a path) must route around failures dynamically, give loop-free paths most of the time, know when a path or destination is unavailable, respect both administrative and user policies, match the requested quality of service, and keep inter- and intra-AS route synthesis independent.

Forwarding decouples inter- and intra-AS decisions, refuses to forward datagrams that are administratively inappropriate or headed to failed resources, and considers destination, quality of service, precedence, policy and security. Information requirements ask for a distributed information base, timely knowledge of resource availability, restrained routing traffic and limited exchange when policy demands it.

The environment requirements include packet switching, connection-less transport, accommodating 10K autonomous systems and 100K networks, and arbitrary interconnection of autonomous systems. General objectives add timeliness, support for systems with limited resources, tolerance of differences in addressing, and that the design must be implementable by network vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: find a way around broken roads, do not send traffic in circles, follow each owner's rules, and be able to cope with ten thousand big networks.

sections.title: Explicit Non-Goals
sections.content:
Because many goals conflict, the memo also says what it is not trying to achieve at this time: ubiquity (every system reaching every other, since cooperation of intermediate resources cannot be guaranteed under policy routing), congestion control, load splitting, maximizing resource utilization, schedule-to-deadline service, and policies based on non-interference such as letting outsiders use spare bandwidth.

The appendix explains some of the reasoning. Load-based routing is called delicate and prone to instability, and non-interference policies would risk routing oscillations and looping. Section 5 adds that transition from the current environment should favor coexistence over a coordinated upgrade, and that it is very unlikely all hosts could be changed.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of things the system does not have to do keeps the job small enough to finish, such as promising that every network can reach every other.

sections.title: Architecture Issues in the Appendix
sections.content:
The appendix defines a boundary gateway as an autonomous system gateway with a network interface directly reachable from another AS, and an interior gateway as any other gateway. It says the Inter-Autonomous System Routing Protocol (IARP) should tolerate an AS whose own routing is unstable, should not force any one interior protocol, and should allow arbitrary topology; the restrictions of the "core model" used by EGP are called unacceptable.

It describes "routing firewalls" that insulate each AS, and three ways to carry transit traffic between boundary gateways: direct connection, tunneling by source routing or encapsulation, or interior gateways that take part in inter-AS routing. The IARP must be able to work as if the boundary gateways were directly connected. Once a packet is allowed into an AS, that AS is expected to deliver it without relying on inter-AS routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Each big network has a few doors to the outside. Those doors talk to other networks' doors, while everything inside stays private and keeps working even if outside gets messy.

sections.title: Policy, Service and Size Discussion
sections.content:
The appendix discusses policy: transit access control, administrative policy and security restrictions can cause a possible explosive growth of routes, so allowing only a smaller subset of constraints may be needed. On service, it argues that type-of-service routing should start with delay, throughput and cost, measured from physical channel characteristics rather than instantaneous load, and that reliability is left out. Multipath routing is desirable but not absolutely required.

On size, it notes that in January 1988 there were more than 330 operational networks and more than 700 network assigned numbers, and that if doubling each year continued, 10,000 nets would be reached near January 1993. A single layer is thought to handle on the order of 10 thousand objects, so the IARP must handle larger internets. It also asks for simple configuration and precise specifications, possibly with pseudo-code or a formal description technique. The memo says security issues are not addressed.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors worry that too many private rules would make route lists explode, and that the Internet was doubling in size every year, so the design must be ready to grow.
